For comparing more than two populations, we employed the Kruskal-Wallis test. To perform post-hoc power analysis for the aforementioned tests, we used Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the empirical power of Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests. You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

We examined 414 columns across 7 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Background: Proper adoption of AI in emergency medicine necessitate thorough and rigorous appraisal.

Classic benchmarks, which rely heavily on basic question-and-answer formats, though dominating the benchmarking field of LLM usage in medicine, have proven inadequate in assessing the full spectrum of skills incumbent upon an agent in healthcare.
Methods: We propose an intricate benchmarking scheme in which the skill set required of an emergency physician is tested and quantified.

Our benchmarking structure is 3-fold: skills such as history taking, diagnostic accuracy, treatment plan, and empathy are evaluated by an emergency medicine expert, while the same expertise is scored by an intern from the perspective of a patient, through what we call a simulated emergency room visit.
A comprehensive written examination is also utilized to measure general emergency medicine knowledge.
Results: Eight LLMs were benchmarked against each other and in contrast to nine emergency medical doctors.
Our findings indicate that the AI models significantly outperformed human physicians across several key domains, including history taking, investigation, diagnostic accuracy, and treatment planning.
Furthermore, the models demonstrated superior performance in comprehensibility, credibility, and empathy.
When comparing AI models against each other, performance advantages were marginal during simulated emergency room visits and were mostly pronounced during the written examination.
Conclusion: AI models demonstrate a clear advantage over human physicians across a diverse range of emergency medicine competencies.
The proposed benchmarking scheme provides a comprehensive metric for a thorough evaluation of medical skill set, furthering validation, adaptation, and utilization of AI in emergency medicine.

Background Diagnostic error, i.e., a clinician's oversight of a diagnosis or failure to reach a correct one in a timely manner, is a pervasive global occurrence and among the prime causes of preventable harm in the healthcare system [1, 2].

text.text: In emergency medicine (EM), rapid and accurate information gathering, decision-making and treatment planning are of paramount importance.

However, the heuristics of emergency medical doctors are constantly under disruptive pressure from the high-stakes nature of EM; doctors have to make multitudinous life-saving decisions under time pressures and in disorderly situations.

text.text: Alongside the explosive advancements of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the widespread utilization in different fields, it has been incorporated in EM as well.
Specific sub-classes of AI, e.g., Large Language Models (LLMs), are suited for tasks such as gathering information and clinical decision-making.
By integrating LLM assistance, one could subdue the eroding factors of working in EM, culminating in the reduction of diagnostic errors [3, 4].

text.text: In this paper, we propose an extensive evaluation process to measure an LLM's medical capabilities in the ED.

Our benchmarking approach is based on simulating EM; by putting an LLM in simulated emergency scenarios as an EM clinician, not only can the medical knowledge and diagnostic proficiencies be analyzed, but we can also properly evaluate the other necessary skills, such as historytaking or empathy [20].

text.text: To establish a baseline to compare the LLMs against, we employed nine EM physicians with different levels of expertise: three residents in early years of residency, three last-year residents, and three emergency medicine specialists.

The selected physicians were compared against eight different LLMs, namely ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, Claude 4.8 Opus, DeepSeek R1, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, O3, Qwen 3.7 Max (Fast), and Qwen 3.7 Max (Thinking), all accessed in June 2026.
To achieve an adequate emulation, we utilized real emergency cases that have occurred in the ED.

Making use of the book "100 Cases in Emergency Medicine and Critical Care" [21], we randomly 1 chose thirty emergency cases, three cases for EM simulation (one per clinician in the three-person groups of residents and specialists) and twenty-seven for the written exam.
text.formatted: Making use of the book "100 Cases in Emergency Medicine and Critical Care" <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, we randomly 1 chose thirty emergency cases, three cases for EM simulation (one per clinician in the three-person groups of residents and specialists) and twenty-seven for the written exam.

text.text: The twenty-seven randomly choses cases, each followed by two to three questions, were provided to the eight LLMs, and their corresponding answers were retrieved.

For testing the human doctors, each clinician was tested with 9 out of 27 cases, in a way that each group (residents, last-year residents, and specialists) would be tested with all 27 cases in the exam questionnaire.
Written answers from clinicians were also retrieved.
Both the answers of the LLMs and clinicians were given to the emergency medicine specialist expert to score on aspects such as diagnosis, investigation, and treatment (Fig 1A).
text.formatted: Both the answers of the LLMs and clinicians were given to the emergency medicine specialist expert to score on aspects such as diagnosis, investigation, and treatment (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1A</ref>).

text.text: For each physician in the experiment, we recruited an intern to represent an emulated patient in an ED case.
After being informed and instructed about the case, each intern, acting as an emergency patient, was interviewed by one human physician and eight different LLMs.
All the interviews were in Farsi language and performed through a mediator, so that the interns wouldn't know if they were being interviewed by a human doctor or AI.
All the clinicians, interns, and LLMs were instructed beforehand on how the experiment was performed and what was expected from them.
After each interview, the intern was provided with a feedback form to rate the interview from different aspects, such as diagnosis, concern reduction, or treatment plan, on a 5-point Likert scale.

In addition, the written records of the interviews were given to an emergency medicine specialist expert to rate the performance of clinicians and LLMs on different criteria, namely history taking, diagnostic accuracy, treatment plan, and the level of empathy.
Names were removed from the interview records; hence, the expert was blinded to the identity of the interviewer, human or LLM (Fig 1B).
text.formatted: Names were removed from the interview records; hence, the expert was blinded to the identity of the interviewer, human or LLM (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1B</ref>).

text.text: All the gathered data in this work is in the format of a 5-point Likert scale, which means that in this work we deal with ordinal data.
Therefore, we generally utilized nonparametric methods for processing and analyzing the data.
We used the Mann-Whitney U test to compare Likert scores from two different groups.
For comparing more than two populations, we employed the Kruskal-Wallis test.
To perform post-hoc power analysis for the aforementioned tests, we used Monte Carlo simulation to estimate the empirical power of Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests.

Simulated Doctor Visit refers to results that are acquired from EM simulation, resulting from the EM expert scoring the interview records.

text.text: As is evident from the charts and the results of the statistical tests, LLMs scored predominantly higher in almost all categories.

In every single category the written exam, LLMs scored significantly higher than physicians, with the p values suggesting an extremely significant difference, i.e., p < 0.001, marked by three asterisks (Fig 2C), and post-hoc power analysis estimating empirical power at ~1.

text.text: When acquiring simulated patients' feedback after each visit, we queried about their opinion regarding the similarity of the doctor, human or AI, to a human.
Patients graded this similarity on a 5-point Likert scale, with 1 meaning a very artificial and 'robotic' interaction and 5 referring to a very natural and human-like interaction.
Since LLMs were instructed not to reveal that they are AI, and the patients were blinded to the identity of their visiting doctors, this score worked as a Turing test [22].

text.text: Ironically, from patients' point of view, the only category with non-significant difference between human physicians and LLMs was human similarity (Fig 2B).

text.text: However, having multiple groups of results, each one with multiple subgroups and categories, represents a complex data structure which makes it difficult to properly quantify the differences among LLMs.
Using machine learning and data mining approaches, we aimed to simplify the data structure, extract the relevant information, and calculate the performance differences.
Firstly, we used factor analysis to extract the underlying factors in the data, so that data dimensions are reduced while relevant information is retained.
Scree plots show that there is one underlying factor in simulated doctor visit scores, one in simulated patient experience scores, and three in written exam resulting data (Fig S3).
text.formatted: Scree plots show that there is one underlying factor in simulated doctor visit scores, one in simulated patient experience scores, and three in written exam resulting data (Fig <ref type="figure">S3</ref>).

text.text: We used factor analysis to extract the underlying factors in doctor visit and patient experience data sets.
As for written exam data, we averaged over diagnosis, investigation, and treatment categories to have three interpretable dimensions of data.
We then used linear regression modeling on this 5-dimensional data, 5-dimensions being the dependent variables and the type of LLM used as independent or explanatory variable.
As is common in the field, we used the performance of ChatGPT in our experiment as the reference and compared the performance of other LLMs against it.

In the fitted linear regression models, each LLM in our work is represented by one term in the models, and the corresponding coefficients are plotted in a forest plot and an accompanying table (Fig 3).

text.text: Comprehensive benchmarks have been implemented to evaluate AI in the context of EM.
They range from simple approaches that assess a singular skill to holistic frameworks that quantify the competence of AI from multiple angles [11, 25].
text.formatted: They range from simple approaches that assess a singular skill to holistic frameworks that quantify the competence of AI from multiple angles <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: Most usually took the same approach: compiling a compendium of questions and tasks, aiming to make each dataset larger than the state of the art, with the goal of covering as many necessary EM skills as possible while circumventing challenges such as data leakage [26, 27].
text.formatted: Most usually took the same approach: compiling a compendium of questions and tasks, aiming to make each dataset larger than the state of the art, with the goal of covering as many necessary EM skills as possible while circumventing challenges such as data leakage <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27]</ref>.

text.text: We took a different approach, however; rather than separately and explicitly testing AI for each specific skill, we aimed to simulate EM and place AI in the simulation.
This way, all necessary skills are intrinsically tested, and the results more accurately reflect real-world performance.
The results demonstrated a clear advantage for the tested AI compared to the human physicians.
LLMs scored significantly higher in skills such as history taking, investigation, diagnosis, treatment plan, comprehensibility, credibility, concern reduction, and empathy.
Unlike the clear contrast between the performances of LLMs and human physicians, the medical expertise among different LLMs was not distinguishable as clearly.
In general, some AI models scored higher than others, but the differences were minor and non-significant.

The only clear distinction was observed in the written exam, in which ChatGPT, O3, Claude, and DeepSeek V4 performed better than Qwen and Gemini, and DeepSeek R1 performed almost universally worse than others.
Findings were consistent between EM simulation and written exam results.
However, there were evaluation aspects that only became evident in the simulation scenarios.
Interview length was a variable factor for instance: on average, Gemini reached a diagnosis after asking 6 questions, Claude after around 9, and ChatGPT or O3 after about 12 questions.
Since there were no significant differences among LLMs in their history taking and diagnosis scores (Fig S1A-I), the higher interview pace suggests a nimbler conduct.
text.formatted: Since there were no significant differences among LLMs in their history taking and diagnosis scores (Fig <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S1A-I</ref>), the higher interview pace suggests a nimbler conduct.

text.text: In the high-stakes, chaotic environment of EM, agile performance is a great asset.
Additionally, quicker diagnosis signifies far fewer tokens spent.
At scale, such disparity can translate to differences in cost and the required resources.
Since the medical competence benchmarking was done in Farsi, it simultaneously operated as a linguistic bias test.
English is the most common language in LLM training, resulting in a bias toward this language [28] [29] [30].
text.formatted: English is the most common language in LLM training, resulting in a bias toward this language <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Analyzing how an AI handles a less common language provides a window into how language bias can affect the interaction quality of LLMs.
In our experiments, LLMs handled Farsi communication well for the most part, as reflected in the high comprehensibility scores by the simulated patients (Fig 2).
text.formatted: In our experiments, LLMs handled Farsi communication well for the most part, as reflected in the high comprehensibility scores by the simulated patients (Fig <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: It seemed that most LLMs performed in their original language (English or Chinese, depending on the origin of the LLM), and translated the message in either the last or first stage.
Therefore, the quality of the conversation was dependent on the quality of the translation.
In rare cases, LLMs produced calques, reducing the quality of the translation.
For example, in one instance, in an attempt to provide reassurance, Claude literally translated the term "you are in good hands" to Farsi, which became meaningless and resulted in patient confusion.
Linguistic bias can be classified as a sub-category of cultural bias.

On a broader scale, training a language model predominantly in one language and attempting to interact with humans in another can hinder the quality of communication due to the inherent cultural discrepancy between the languages.
An example of such bias was the frequent attempts by one of the LLMs to reassure or empathize, which made a simulated patient feel uneasy and doubtful.
He was used to interacting with direct and to-thepoint doctors, and his interaction with the LLM felt dishonest and insincere.

This sentiment was supported by some others during our experiments, leading us to believe that developing one model and using translation to utilize it in different countries might result in impaired communications.
If the aim is to deploy a medical AI system on a commercial scale that can properly interact with the patients, adaptations based on the target country are needed.
Since their inception, LLMs have been marred by hallucinations.
With each new iteration of an LLM, measures have been taken to reduce the rate of hallucinations [31].
text.formatted: With each new iteration of an LLM, measures have been taken to reduce the rate of hallucinations <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Considering all the different LLMs that have been thoroughly tested in the medical context, this work provided an apt testing environment for hallucination occurrence.
During the patient interviews in the course of the EM simulation, no hallucinations were detected.
We speculate this is because most of the LLMs used in this work are rather new, and have modern mitigation strategies to prevent hallucinations.

The same was true during the written exam benchmarking, with the exception of Claude 4.8 Opus; when the questions in the written exam were given to Claude all together, it answered the first few, then started hallucinating new questions answering its own made-up questions.
Multiple tries resulted in the same outcome, forcing us to divide the written exam into smaller batches of questions and gather the answers batch-wise.
This shows that while the hallucination rate has been reduced drastically in newer LLMs, they still occur.
In medicine, these occurrences can have drastic consequences, necessitating further improvement in hallucination prevention.
In this work, we have demonstrated how novel benchmarking approaches can provide better insights into AI performance in distinctive applications.
The added insight comes at a price, however, warranting extra time and resources compared to automated Q&A-based methods.
text.formatted: The added insight comes at a price, however, warranting extra time and resources compared to automated Q&A-based methods.

text.text: A potential countermeasure for the costly steps would be to partially automate the framework.
Admittedly, major ethical, legal, and regulatory challenges for the fully automated benchmarks persist [1].
text.formatted: Admittedly, major ethical, legal, and regulatory challenges for the fully automated benchmarks persist <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Yet, approaches such as humanin-the-loop artificial intelligence solutions can mitigate these challenges by balancing automation efficiency with human oversight and improve accuracy beyond unassisted human or AI performance alone [32].
text.formatted: Yet, approaches such as humanin-the-loop artificial intelligence solutions can mitigate these challenges by balancing automation efficiency with human oversight and improve accuracy beyond unassisted human or AI performance alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Predictive models can also circumvent some steps which are time-and resource-costly.
A solution to use publicly available benchmarking results to predict AI competence in EM is explored in the supplements (S4 and Fig S2).
text.formatted: A solution to use publicly available benchmarking results to predict AI competence in EM is explored in the supplements (S4 and Fig <ref type="figure">S2</ref>).

text.text: AI advancements were astonishing in the past few years.
In this work, AI could outperform human physicians in almost every metric (Fig 2).
text.formatted: In this work, AI could outperform human physicians in almost every metric (Fig <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Even in a metric such as the human similarity, AI performed quite well, indicating that patients found AI and human doctors indistinguishable.
The widespread utilization of such competent medical tools might be enticing to the stakeholders.
However, any mishap tracing back to impetuous AI employment can have devastating repercussions for the AI acclimation in medicine [10].
text.formatted: However, any mishap tracing back to impetuous AI employment can have devastating repercussions for the AI acclimation in medicine <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Though still limited, negative perception is growing against AI in medicine, due to the usage of imperfect AI programs by some U.S. health insurers and the subsequent sinister effect on patients' medical care [33, 34].
text.formatted: Though still limited, negative perception is growing against AI in medicine, due to the usage of imperfect AI programs by some U.S. health insurers and the subsequent sinister effect on patients' medical care <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34]</ref>.

text.text: Decision-makers shall tread carefully, establish stringent regulations, and employ thorough verification if they want to avoid similar unfortunate incidents in emergency medicine.
